scenario: AITA for not hosting thanksgiving like I planned to | For about 50 years, my mom hosted all of her children and grandchildren for thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. She’s now gotten too old and asked us kids to take over the tradition. There are 4 of us so we just rotate. We’ve each hosted one holiday so far. This thanksgiving is my turn. We have never spent thanksgiving or Christmas Eve with my wife’s family. We’ve just never been as close to them plus they live all over the country. Well this year her mom and aunts decided to go to the Macy’s thanksgiving day parade. At first it was just a sister’s trip but then they decided to invite all their kids and grandkids to meet them up there. My wife really wants to go. She hasnt seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter wants to go because it’s a “once in a lifetime event” (which i agree with). And I want to go. As soon as we decided to go I called my older brother to see what we should do about thanksgiving because I can’t host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

prediction.raw: This is a **1**—you’re **not in the wrong** for prioritizing your family’s happiness and your wife’s emotional needs, especially when the situation is unique and time-sensitive. Here’s why: ### **Why It’s Okay (or Even Responsible)** 1. **Family Bonds Matter More Than Tradition** – Your mom’s tradition was built on love and connection, but that doesn’t mean it’s *rigid*. If your wife and daughter have a rare opportunity to reconnect with their family, that’s a meaningful experience worth making room for. Your mom would likely want you to prioritize joy and closeness over rigid expectations. 2. **You Offered Solutions** – You tried to compensate (renting a space, hosting next time), but your sister rejected those because she wanted the *experience* of hosting, not just the logistics. That’s her choice, not a reflection of your effort. 3. **It’s Not "Abandoning" Thanksgiving** – Your sister’s anger seems rooted in guilt (for not stepping up) and frustration (that she’s now stuck hosting). But you’re not abandoning the holiday—you’re adapting it to fit a real, once-in-a-lifetime moment for your wife and daughter. 4. **Your Mom Would Understand** – If your mom were alive, she’d likely say: *"Go. Be happy. Family is about love, not just tradition."* She’d want you to cherish these moments, not resent them. 5. **Your Brother’s Hesitation Isn’t Your Fault** – If he’s not supportive, that’s his issue, not yours. You’re not obligated to make him comfortable—you’re making *your* family happy. ### **Where You *Might* Have Room to Improve** - **Communication Tone** – Your sister’s anger might soften if you framed it as: *"I’m so excited for us to go, but I know how much this means to Mom. Can we figure out a way to honor her memory while making this work?"* (Instead of just saying, *"I’m doing this."*) - **Offering to Host Next Time** – If she’s still upset, you could say: *"I’d love to host Christmas next year if that helps ease your mind."* (But don’t push—she may just need time to process.) ### **Final Verdict** You’re **not wrong**—you’re making a thoughtful, loving choice. The guilt you’re feeling comes from societal pressure to "follow tradition at all costs," but real family love is flexible. Your wife and daughter’s happiness (and your own) matter just as much as the tradition. Would you like help drafting a message to your sister to soften the blow? Or are you leaning toward just accepting that this year’s dynamic is different? Either way, you’re handling it with care. 💛
